help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 5: Mixtures and Solubility.
Orange juice, oatmeal and smoothies are all mixtures.
Stir sugar into tea, and it dissolves,
until the tea can't hold any more.
In this unit, we'll explore pure substances, mixtures, how to separate them,
and how things dissolve.
Everything around us is matter,
and it can be sorted into pure substances and mixtures.
Pure substances are either elements or compounds.
An element, like gold or neon, can't be broken down by chemical reactions.
There are 118 known elements.
A compound forms when elements join chemically in a fixed ratio, like water,
H2O, or salt, NaCl.
Its properties are different from its elements,
and it can only be separated by chemical methods.
A mixture contains substances that are not chemically joined, in any proportions,
so they can be separated by physical methods.
Mixtures are either homogeneous or heterogeneous.
In a heterogeneous mixture, 'hetero' means different: the parts are not evenly spread,
and you can see them.
Soil, sand and water, and oil and water are heterogeneous.
In a homogeneous mixture, 'homo' means the same: the parts are evenly spread,
in one state, and you can't tell them apart.
Salt water, air and steel are homogeneous.
A solution is a homogeneous mixture.
The substance that dissolves, like sugar, is the solute.
The substance that does the dissolving, like water, is the solvent.
A pure substance contains only one type of atom or molecule.
Mixtures aren't pure, but we can describe the purity of one part:
how much of it there is compared to the whole mixture.
Bottled water often contains added minerals, so it isn't 100 percent pure water,
but it's still safe to drink.
We calculate percentage purity like this: the mass of the pure substance,
divided by the total mass of the mixture, times 100.
A bronze coin has a mass of 75 grams,
and 62 grams of it is copper.
62 divided by 75, times 100, is about 82.7 percent copper.
Purity matters: medicines need exactly the right amount of active ingredient,
and dental implants use very pure metals to avoid allergic reactions.
Jewellers describe the purity of gold in carats.
Here is the percentage of gold in four common types.
24 carat gold is almost pure: 99.9 percent gold.
18 carat gold is only 75 percent gold;
the rest is other metals such as copper or silver.
Pause and decide: a ring of 18 carat gold has a mass of 8 grams.
What mass of gold does it contain?

captions: Because mixtures aren't chemically joined, we can separate them physically.
Handpicking removes large pieces by hand or with forceps.
Sieving separates large particles from small ones: the small ones fall through.
Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid.
The liquid passes through filter paper and is collected as the filtrate,
while the solid stays behind as the residue.
Evaporation separates a dissolved solute from a solution.
Heat it, the solvent evaporates, and the solute is left behind,
like salt from salt water.
Distillation collects the solvent.
The mixture is heated; the substance with the lowest boiling point evaporates first,
then cools and condenses back into a liquid, called the distillate.
This can turn salt water into pure water.
A dot of black felt-tip ink is put on a
pencil line near the bottom of a strip of paper.
The bottom edge stands in water.
Predict: will the ink stay as one black
spot as the water soaks up the paper?
Pause and decide.
Watch. The water soaks slowly up the paper, past the ink spot.
The black ink separates into three coloured spots at different heights:
yellow at the top, then red, then blue.
Explain what you saw.
Black ink is a mixture of dyes.
Each dye dissolves in the water,
but travels up the paper at a different speed, so the dyes separate.
The yellow dye moved furthest.
This method is paper chromatography.
A pure substance would give only one spot.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Chromatography separates substances that dissolve in the same solvent,
like the dyes in ink.
Draw a pencil line near the bottom of special paper,
add a dot of ink,
and dip the end in a solvent such as water or alcohol,
keeping the line above the solvent.
As the solvent soaks up the paper, it carries the dyes with it.
Each dye travels at a different speed, so they separate into spots.
The result is called a chromatogram.
This brown ink contains three dyes: blue, red and yellow.
A pure substance gives just one spot, like this red ink.
Chromatography is used to check the nutritional value of food, measure blood glucose,
and test water for pollution.

captions: Solutions are everywhere: lemonade, rubbing alcohol and the saline used in hospitals.
Concentration tells us how much solute is dissolved in a given amount of solvent.
More solute particles in the same volume means a higher concentration.
Add more sugar to lemonade, and it gets sweeter!
To calculate concentration, divide the mass of the solute by the volume of the solution.
5 grams of sugar in 100 cubic centimetres gives 0.05 grams per cubic centimetre.
Keep adding sugar to water, and eventually no more will dissolve.
The solution is saturated.
Before that point, it's unsaturated.
A supersaturated solution holds more than it normally can, so it's unstable,
and crystals form.
Solubility is how much solute can dissolve in a solvent.
For most solids, it increases with temperature.
At 10 degrees Celsius, one sugar cube might saturate the water,
but at 40 degrees, three cubes can dissolve.
That's why it's easier to dissolve sugar in hot tea.
Here's a graph of solubility against temperature.
Different substances have different solubilities,
but they all rise as the water gets hotter.
When testing this, keep everything the same except the temperature,
to make it a fair test.
This graph shows the maximum mass of potassium nitrate,
a salt used in fertilisers,
that dissolves in 100 grams of water at different temperatures.
At 20 degrees Celsius, only 32 grams dissolve.
At 60 degrees, 110 grams dissolve.
The curve gets steeper:
solubility rises faster and faster as the water gets hotter.
Pause and decide: a saturated solution in 100 grams of
water at 60 degrees is cooled to 20 degrees.
What mass of crystals forms?

Question 1: Is salt water a homogeneous or heterogeneous mixture?

Answer: Homogeneous – the salt is evenly spread.
Question 2: Which method separates tea leaves from tea?

Answer: Filtration.
Question 3: A chromatogram of an ink shows one spot.
What does this tell you?

Answer: The ink is a pure substance.
Question 4: Why does more sugar dissolve in hot water than in cold water?
